reports.summary: TPTL is India's leading high-speed gearbox manufacturer with a unique position in naval defence propulsion systems, benefiting from the Indian Navy's indigenisation push targeting 175-200 ships by 2035. The company combines best-in-class 35%+ EBITDA margins, a strong order book of 1.8x revenue (60% defence), and significant operating leverage from a Rs 3bn capacity expansion. With 21% revenue CAGR and 19% EBITDA CAGR projected through FY29E, TPTL offers multi-year visibility through both repeat OEM orders and defence execution.
reports.connection_narrative: India's naval expansion is structurally accelerating with capex more than doubling from Rs 267bn in FY21 to Rs 625bn in FY26, driven by a policy imperative to reach 175-200 ships by 2035. The critical bottleneck in indigenisation lies in the 'Move' category—propulsion and power systems—which are only 60% localised compared to 90% for hulls, making this the government's primary focus for manufacturing relocation. Simultaneously, global supply chain fragmentation and geopolitical tension have accelerated OEMs' appetite for qualified suppliers outside Europe, while India's export thrust into high-value engineering niches is receiving fiscal and policy support. Triveni Power Transmission operates at the intersection of all three macro drivers: it is among the few domestic companies qualified in both propulsion gearboxes and propulsion shafting—the two critical 'Move' components—and holds sticky OEM approvals from Siemens, Everllence, and Mitsubishi that generate recurring orders. Its 25-30% cost advantage and 6-8 month delivery versus 12+ months for European competitors position it to capture share as global customers diversify sourcing and as Indian shipyards scale production. The aftermarket business, contributing 31% of revenue, provides recurring, high-margin revenue that stabilises cash flows and enables TPTL to maintain industry-leading 35%+ EBITDA margins despite executing longer-duration defence contracts at lower initial margins. A Rs 3bn capacity expansion has doubled gears capacity to Rs 7bn—roughly 2x FY26 revenue—with much of the fixed cost already embedded in the P&L, creating significant operating leverage as utilisation rises from below 50% today. The immediate catalyst is accelerating defence order flow from the Navy and Mazagon Dock as shipyard production ramps, while the key downside risk is execution delays in defence programmes or a slower-than-expected Navy capex release cycle, both of which could compress near-term EBITDA margins despite the strong order book.
